issues.legal_issue: A retired government employee has no entitlement to retain government accommodation or receive alternative government accommodation without a policy authorizing it.
material_facts: A government employee who had been displaced by terrorism retired while occupying government accommodation.

After retirement, he sought to retain that accommodation indefinitely for a nominal licence fee and the High Courts directed that eviction be kept in abeyance and alternative accommodation be provided.
No government policy authorized allotment of government accommodation to displaced retired employees; the accommodation was intended for serving officials.
issues.conclusion: The High Court directions were unsustainable. A retired government employee cannot retain government accommodation or demand alternative government accommodation in the absence of a policy authorizing it.
issues.legal_principle: Government accommodation is scarce public property intended for serving officials, not retirees. In S.D. Bandi v. Divisional Traffic Officer (2013) 12 SCC 631, Shiv Sagar Tiwari v. Union of India (1997) 1 SCC 444, and Lok Prahari (I) v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2016) 8 SCC 389 and Lok Prahari (II) v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 6 SCC 1, the Court rejected unauthorized or policy-free allotment and retention of government residences, including by former public officeholders. Compassion does not itself create an entitlement to public property or authorize a court to direct an allotment unsupported by policy.

predicates.appeal_challenges_housing_order_for_reti: An appeal challenges a court order allowing a retired public official to retain or receive government housing.
predicates.official_has_retired: The public official whose housing entitlement is at issue has retired from government service.
predicates.official_seeks_to_retain_or_receive_gove: The retired official has sought to keep government housing or obtain alternative government housing.
predicates.no_policy_authorizes_housing_for_retired: No government policy authorizes the allotment of government housing to retired officials in the circumstances at issue.
predicates.government_housing_is_for_serving_offici: The government housing at issue is provided for officials serving in government employment.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a housing order for a retired official who seeks government housing, no policy authorizes that housing, and the housing is for serving officials, the retired official is not entitled to government housing.

issues.legal_issue: The right to shelter does not entitle a displaced retired public employee to government housing when the applicable policy provides for transit accommodation or cash assistance.
material_facts: The retired employee had been displaced from his home by terrorism and relied on the right to shelter to seek continued or alternative government housing.
The government policy for displaced persons provided for transit accommodation and, where that accommodation was unavailable, cash assistance toward rental and incidental expenses.
The employee had received a salary, pension and retirement benefits, and the Court noted that the policy-based shelter response did not include government quarters for displaced retirees.
issues.conclusion: The right to shelter does not extend to a right to government accommodation. The applicable provision of transit accommodation or cash assistance addresses the displaced person’s shelter needs, and hardship alone does not impose a duty on the State to provide government housing.
issues.legal_principle: Although the right to shelter is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution, it does not create an indefeasible right to government accommodation. The Court distinguished the accommodation relief in J.L. Koul v. State of J&K (2010) 1 SCC 371, which concerned a rehabilitation scheme and was granted on its particular facts. It also rejected the broader approach taken in Union of India v. Vijay Mam (2012 SCC OnLine Del 3218): compassion and hardship cannot justify allotting government property without a supporting policy.

rule.if: displaced_person_shelter_claim and claimant_is_retired_public_employee and claimant_seeks_government_housing_under_shelter_right and policy_provides_transit_housing_or_cash and no_policy_authorizes_government_housing_for_displaced_retirees

predicates.displaced_person_shelter_claim: A displaced person seeks accommodation on the basis of a claim to shelter.
predicates.claimant_is_retired_public_employee: The person making the shelter claim is a retired government employee.
predicates.claimant_seeks_government_housing_under_: The claimant relies on the right to shelter to seek government housing.
predicates.policy_provides_transit_housing_or_cash: The applicable policy provides transit accommodation or cash assistance toward housing expenses for displaced persons.
predicates.no_policy_authorizes_government_housing_: No policy authorizes government housing for displaced retired employees in the circumstances at issue.

issues.definition: When a displaced retired public employee seeks government housing under the right to shelter, the applicable policy provides transit housing or cash, and no policy authorizes government housing for such retirees, the shelter right does not entitle the claimant to government housing.

issues.legal_issue: Relief granted by the Supreme Court under its complete-justice jurisdiction on special facts does not constitute binding precedent for a later claim to the same relief.
material_facts: A prior Supreme Court order had allowed certain retired displaced persons to continue occupying accommodation pending implementation of a rehabilitation scheme.
That order accepted a state rehabilitation scheme and was made under the Supreme Court’s complete-justice jurisdiction on the circumstances before it.
The High Courts relied on that relief as support for directing continued or alternative government accommodation in a later case.
issues.conclusion: The prior order was a direction under Article 142 of the Constitution on special facts, not a binding precedent establishing a general entitlement to government accommodation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding; relief fashioned under Article 142 on peculiar facts does not, without a declaration of law, establish a binding rule for other cases. Indian Bank v. ABS Marine Products (P) Ltd. (2006) 5 SCC 72 cautions courts to follow the ratio decidendi rather than a fact-specific relaxation of relief. Ram Pravesh Singh v. State of Bihar (2006) 8 SCC 381 likewise holds that a direction made under Article 142 on special facts is not binding precedent.

rule.if: later_case_relies_on_prior_supreme_court_relief and prior_relief_was_granted_on_special_facts and prior_order_used_complete_justice_power and prior_order_declared_no_general_rule

predicates.later_case_relies_on_prior_supreme_court: A court in a later case relies on relief previously granted by the Supreme Court.
predicates.prior_relief_was_granted_on_special_fact: The earlier relief was based on the particular circumstances of that case.
predicates.prior_order_used_complete_justice_power: The Supreme Court granted the earlier relief in exercising its power to do complete justice.
predicates.prior_order_declared_no_general_rule: The earlier order did not declare a general legal rule governing other cases.

issues.definition: When a later case relies on Supreme Court relief granted on special facts under its complete-justice power, and the order declared no general rule, that relief is not binding precedent.
